newsitem.title: USA: Iowa corn and soybean crops in mostly good shape.
newsitem.headline: Iowa corn and soybean crops in mostly good shape.

text.p: The following is the weekly crop summary from the Iowa Agricultural Statistics Service for the week ending August 3.

Mild weather prevailed through the workweek with very warm and humid conditions dominating the weekend. Temperature extremes ranged from a Thursday (31st) morning low of 48 degrees at Fayette to afternoon highs of 95 degrees at Marshalltown on Saturday (2nd) and at Cedar Rapids, Denison, Guthrie Center, Oakland, and Winterset on Sunday (3rd). Temperatures for the week as a whole averaged one to two degrees below normal. Approximately two-thirds of Iowa failed to receive any measurable rain during the week. Scattered rain fell over the southern quarter of the state on Monday (28th) and over the northwest quarter of Iowa on Thursday (31st). Thunderstorms were also scattered over north central and southwestern Iowa on Friday (1st). Finally, southern and eastern portions of the state received some isolated downpours on Sunday (3rd) with a few areas receiving hail and high winds in east central Iowa. The greatest reported weekly rain totals were 1.43 inches at the Quad Cities, 1.14 inches at De Witt (Clinton County), 0.78 inch at Dorchester (Allamakee County), 0.75 inch at Donnellson (Lee County), and 0.72 inch at Hancock (Pottawattamie County). The state average precipitation was only 0.09 inch or about one-tenth of the weekly normal of 0.88 inch.

Iowa's corn and soybean crops continue to be in mostly good condition, even though some are dealing with low moisture and high insect populations. Harvesting of the oat crop and moving old-crop grains were the main activities for crop farmers this past week. Farmers are still hoping for some good rain in the near future to maintain crop development. A variety of insects have invaded Iowa's crops this season. Reporters in the north central and the three southern districts note damage from grasshoppers is significant. Leafhoppers are still causing damage to alfalfa in the north central, northeast, and southwest districts. Spider mites are being reported in west central, east central, and southwest soybean fields. Corn borers are reported as most prevalent in the west central and central districts. As of Friday, August 1, the state's topsoil moisture was rated 13 percent very short, 35 percent short, 50 percent adequate, and 2 percent surplus. The driest areas are the east central district, where 75 percent of the topsoil was rated short or very short, and the south central district, where 34 percent of the topsoil was rated very short. Subsoil moisture was rated 7 percent very short, 31 percent short, 60 percent adequate, and 2 percent surplus. Statewide, there were 6.0 days suitable for field work last week. Reports from around the state tell a common story-the corn looks good in many areas, but corn in dry areas is showing stress at this time. As of Sunday, August 3, 98 percent of Iowa's corn crop had tasseled, compared to 88 percent last year and 84 percent for the five-year average. Corn silked has reached 92 percent, one week ahead of 1996 and ten days ahead of the five-year average of 73 percent. Fifteen percent of Iowa's corn crop was in the milk stage or beyond as of Sunday. That is nearly four days ahead of last year's pace, but four days behind the five-year average of 22 percent. The corn condition declined from a week ago and was rated 1 percent very poor, 3 percent poor, 19 percent fair, 57 percent good, and 20 percent excellent as of Friday. Soybean acreage blooming in Iowa had reached 95 percent as of Sunday, nearly two weeks ahead of both the five-year average and the 1996 pace. Soybean acreage setting pods is at 58 percent, four days ahead of the five-year average of 46 percent and nearly one week ahead of last year's pace (34 percent). The soybean condition also declined last week and was rated 1 percent very poor, 3 percent poor, 21 percent fair, 59 percent good, and 16 percent excellent as of Friday. Harvesting of the second crop of alfalfa hay was 86 percent complete as of Sunday, one week ahead of last year and nine days ahead of the five-year average. Harvesting of the second crop of clover hay was 48 percent complete. Both the five-year average and last year's pace was 39 percent, four days behind the pace this season. The condition of the hay crop was rated 8 percent very poor, 14 percent poor, 33 percent fair, 38 percent good, and 7 percent excellent as of Friday. Harvesting of oats for grain was 77 percent complete as of Sunday, three days ahead of 1996, when 66 percent had been harvested, and three days ahead of the five-year average of 68 percent. Iowa's winter wheat harvest was 91 percent complete as of Sunday, two days behind the 1996 pace of 95 percent, but five days ahead of the five-year average of 84 percent.

Cooler temperatures through most of the week helped to relieve the heat and humidity stress on livestock. Flies are becoming a problem in the north central district and the eastern third of the state. Some pinkeye was reported in the southern three districts. Statewide, livestock are still considered to be in good condition. As of Friday, pasture conditions declined from last week and were rated 10 percent very poor, 22 percent poor, 34 percent fair, 30 percent good, and 4 percent excellent.
